prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms enabled frequency measurements at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part for B046, Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange sharpened my reasons rather than changing them. In one sentence, what a lattice-clock citation recognises that the comb (2005) and single-system control (2012) did not: the invention of magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the lattice light shift as a systematic and so lets thousands of neutral atoms be interrogated at once, combining ensemble statistics with the small systematic shifts previously available only to single trapped ions, and its realisation at the 1e-18 level. The comb supplied a ruler to count optical cycles; Wineland's ion work supplied control of one quantum system. Neither supplied this trade-off. The maturity evidence is the kind I trust as an experimentalist: independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) reproduce the performance with different species and compare clocks over fibre and free space, so the systematics have been tested by people who did not build the original apparatus, and the instrument already resolves gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale cloud. That is a new observable, not a better number. Two names also map cleanly onto the proposal plus first demonstration (Katori) and the record accuracy and many-body realisation (Ye). I have heard no argument in round 1 that B046 lacks merit, only arguments about kind (discovery versus instrument) and attribution, and on both I think B046 is at least as defensible as the alternatives.
statement.case_against: The honest weak points remain. First, B046 is an invention and measurement advance more than a discovery about nature, and its fundamental-physics output so far is limits (constants, dark matter, geodesy) rather than findings; members who weigh discovery over instrument (Danielsson, Eriksson, Olsson) can reasonably rank B038 higher on that criterion, and I do not claim their criterion is wrong, only that the committee has consistently honoured measurement inventions. Second, it sits in a long metrology line, and the citation must state plainly what is new. Third, a two-name list leaves visible gaps for Lemonde (SYRTE), Takamoto and Ludlow, and the ion-clock groups, and I recall their priority details from memory rather than from the primary papers. Fourth, I carry a personal-scientific proximity to the Ye group (see conflict note) and may over-read a field I know well.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B038 and ranks the lattice clock second; in round 1 she and several others wrote that Ye already shares the 2005 prize, and that the committee might wait for the SI redefinition of the second.
responses.response: The chair asks for the record to be settled, and I will state what I know: the 2005 Physics prize went to Roy Glauber (quantum theory of optical coherence) and to John Hall and Theodor Hansch (laser-based precision spectroscopy including the optical frequency comb). Jun Ye was Hall's postdoctoral researcher and later a JILA fellow, but he was not a laureate. If the committee's own records show otherwise I would like to see them, but I do not think the overlap argument against B046 can stand as 'Ye already has a prize'. The real overlap question is whether the invention is the same chain, and I answer that above. On waiting for the redefinition, I still disagree: the performance is verified now, and tying recognition to a metrology-body timetable adds no scientific information. I also note that a prize that waits risks the credit becoming harder rather than easier as more groups produce record results.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B038 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a verified prediction-to-measurement chain and a new state of matter, and keeps B046 as his second alternative; he would keep the citation narrow to the 2D quantum spin Hall state.
responses.response: I accept the strength of the chain, and I accept the discovery-over-instrument distinction as a legitimate criterion; if the committee applied it strictly, B038 would be my first alternative, and I have moved it there from third place on my list. Where I remain unpersuaded is that B038 resolves its own attribution problem. A citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect pairs Kane and Mele with Molenkamp, yet the experiment tested a specific HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and you yourself say you have no neat answer. Narrowing the wording does not change who told the experimentalists where to look. As an outsider to condensed matter I would defer to you and Olsson if you can show a citation that is honest about that gap; absent that, the two-name B046 credit is the one that needs no such defence. I also accept your point that 2016 is conceptually distinct, so I do not use it against B038.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, leans toward a narrow citation around the invention and is less sure than I am that a third name is needed; he also asks for a defensible position on Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow.
responses.response: I have reconsidered the third-name question and I now come down on a two-name prize. My round-1 openness to a third name was about fairness, but with the three-person cap the choice would be between Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow, and I cannot defend any one over the others from memory. Takamoto's contribution is closely tied to Katori's first Sr lattice clock and is covered by Katori's credit as realisation; the SYRTE work on Sr/Hg lattice clocks was important and independent, but a citation worded around the invention and its first realisation does not require it. I would therefore ask the committee to word the citation on the magic-wavelength lattice, as you suggest, rather than the whole field of optical clocks, and to state in the report that ion clocks and the later accuracy race involved many groups. This is a judgment about wording, not a claim that those contributors were minor.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from WMAP to B038 and argued that the prediction-to-measurement chain is the clearest example of a clue from nature, while listing B046 as an alternative and noting that he would defer to metrology expertise on novelty.
responses.response: Since you defer to metrology expertise on novelty, here is my reading. The novelty is not frequency precision as such but a method that changes what can be measured: many atoms held with the lattice light shift cancelled. The scientific payoff you ask about is already partly there, because redshift across a millimetre-scale sample and species-to-species ratio comparisons are measurements that earlier clocks could not make, and they are what constants and dark-matter searches now use. I concede that these are not yet discoveries. On your own criterion of a discovery whose attribution is unambiguous, I would say B038 is unambiguous in the physics but not in the credit, whereas B046 is the reverse; I think a prize is more robust when credit is clear and the science is already confirmed independently, so I stay with B046 but would not oppose B038 if the condensed-matter members can state the credit honestly.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to B046, and in round 1 argued that the clock is a conceptual step (many atoms interrogated at once) and that circuit QED should be held back after the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree with the conceptual-step wording and would put it in the citation. On circuit QED, your disagreement with me about Blais versus Girvin is itself the argument for holding B006 back: if two committee members cannot agree on the theory slot, the committee cannot yet say who the credit belongs to, and the 2025 prize makes the timing worse. I therefore keep B006 only as a lower alternative. I would, however, still ask the committee not to confuse the platform with the physics: the 2004 strong-coupling result and dispersive readout are the durable contribution, and that should shape any later citation. I also appreciate your being open about your own proximity to that community.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct invention from the comb and single-ion control, or reads B046 as a third prize on one precision-metrology chain; this is a judgment I cannot make for others.

Whether the discovery-versus-instrument criterion should carry more weight than clean attribution; this is the real axis separating B046 from B038, and I defer to condensed-matter members on whether B038 can be credited honestly without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
Priority details for Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow are recalled from memory and have not been checked against the 2003 to 2006 papers.
My own weighting may favour precision measurement more than the committee average.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. In my doctoral period I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, in the 1980s, long before Ye joined Hall as a postdoctoral researcher; Ye later became a JILA fellow, so this is a personal-scientific acquaintance through the Hall group, not a joint project, a supervisory relationship or a shared publication that I know of. My research on spectral-hole-burning crystals and slow-light laser stabilisation touches ultrastable lasers used in clocks, but I have no joint work with Katori or Ye. I declare this and will accept the committee's decision whether I should step back on B046; I have not asked to recuse, and I will not be the sole advocate for the configuration. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers and Johansson, which is relevant only if circuit QED returns to discussion.
